stem: The focus of an earthquake is
a: the point on the surface directly above the rupture
b: the place in the Earth where the rupture begins
c: the instrument that records the shaking
explanation: The focus, or hypocentre, is the underground point where the earthquake starts. The point on the surface above it is the epicentre.

stem: The epicentre is
a: the deepest part of the inner core
d: the point on the surface above the focus
explanation: The epicentre lies on the ground surface vertically above the focus. It is not the underground starting point itself.

stem: A seismograph is
c: an instrument that records ground motion
explanation: A seismograph detects and records shaking. The record it produces is a seismogram.

stem: A seismogram is
explanation: The seismogram is the trace, on paper or in a digital file, made by a seismograph during an earthquake.

stem: P waves are
a: the faster primary waves, which can travel through solids and liquids
explanation: P stands for primary. These compressional waves arrive first and can travel through both solid and liquid material.

stem: S waves are
b: able to cross the liquid outer core
c: sound waves in the air only
d: slower shear waves that do not pass through liquid
explanation: S waves move by shearing, so they need a solid. They are stopped by the liquid outer core, which is why a shadow zone exists.

stem: Which waves usually arrive first at a distant station?
explanation: P waves travel fastest, so they are the first mark on a seismogram. S waves and surface waves follow.

stem: S waves do not travel through the outer core because the outer core is
explanation: Shear waves cannot pass through a liquid. The failure of S waves to cross the outer core is evidence that this layer is molten.

stem: The Richter scale is a measure of
a: the size of the earthquake at its source
b: the damage at one town only, with no regard to the source
explanation: Richter magnitude describes the energy release, based on the amplitude of the waves. The Mercalli scale instead describes the intensity of shaking and damage at a place.

stem: The Mercalli scale describes
a: the exact energy in joules only
c: the age of a rock in years
d: the intensity of shaking and the effects people observe
explanation: Mercalli intensity uses observations such as whether objects fall or buildings crack. It can differ from town to town for the same earthquake.

stem: Magnitude and intensity differ because
a: intensity is measured only at the focus
c: magnitude is one value for the earthquake, while intensity varies from place to place
d: they are two names for the same town report
explanation: An earthquake has a single magnitude. Its intensity is usually greatest near the epicentre and weaker farther away.

stem: A normal fault is typically caused by
d: blocks sliding sideways with no vertical motion only
explanation: In a normal fault the hanging wall moves down relative to the footwall, under tension. Compression produces a reverse fault.

stem: A reverse fault is typically caused by
explanation: Under compression the hanging wall is pushed up relative to the footwall. That is a reverse, or thrust, fault.

stem: A strike-slip fault is one in which the blocks
a: only move straight up and down
c: are separated by a river with no movement
explanation: Motion on a strike-slip fault is mainly sideways. The San Andreas fault is a well-known example.

stem: Most earthquakes occur
c: along the boundaries of tectonic plates
d: only at the centres of stable continents
explanation: Plates grind, collide, or pull apart at their edges, so most quakes are concentrated there. The interiors of plates are much quieter.

stem: The Himalayas are associated with
a: a transform fault with no mountains
b: collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates
c: a mid-ocean ridge in the Arabian Sea only
explanation: The Indian plate is pushing into Eurasia. That continental collision builds the Himalayas and causes earthquakes across the region, including northern Pakistan.

stem: A mid-ocean ridge is a place where plates
a: move apart and new crust is formed
explanation: At a divergent boundary, magma rises and makes new oceanic crust. These ridges also produce earthquakes.

stem: A subduction zone is where
c: the crust is thickest and never moves
explanation: Oceanic crust can be forced down into the mantle. Subduction zones produce deep earthquakes and often volcanoes.

stem: A tsunami is
c: a series of sea waves set off by a large displacement of water, often an undersea earthquake
d: a tidal wave caused only by the Moon
explanation: If the seabed is suddenly raised or dropped, the water column is disturbed and long waves travel outward. These are tsunamis, not ordinary wind waves or tides.

stem: The lag between P and S arrivals increases when the station is
d: at the focus itself, with a large lag
explanation: S waves are slower, so the gap between the two arrivals grows with distance. That gap is used to estimate how far away the earthquake was.

stem: Locating an epicentre commonly needs records from at least
explanation: One station gives a distance, which is a circle of possible places. A second circle narrows it, and a third fixes the point where the circles meet.

stem: Aftershocks are
b: storms that always follow a quake
c: P waves from a different planet
d: smaller earthquakes that follow the main shock
explanation: The crust continues to adjust after the main rupture, producing smaller events. They can still be damaging.

stem: The main shock is
c: the largest earthquake in a sequence
explanation: In a sequence, the event of greatest magnitude is the main shock. Smaller events before it are foreshocks, and those after it are aftershocks.

stem: A foreshock is
b: a smaller earthquake before the main shock
d: a surface wave that arrives first
explanation: Foreshocks are recognised clearly only after the larger main shock has occurred. Not every earthquake has them.

stem: Surface waves travel
a: along the outer part of the Earth
c: faster than P waves through the body of the Earth
d: through the air as ordinary sound
explanation: Love and Rayleigh waves move near the surface. They are often slower than body waves but can cause strong shaking.

stem: Body waves include
explanation: Body waves travel through the interior. P and S are the two kinds. Surface waves are a separate group.

stem: The shadow zone for S waves occurs because
c: S waves cannot cross the liquid outer core
d: P waves stop at the crust
explanation: Beyond a certain distance, S waves are absent because the liquid outer core blocks them. That absence is the S-wave shadow zone.

stem: Seismic waves have shown that Earth's outer core is liquid because
b: S waves do not pass through it
d: surface waves travel only in the core
explanation: S waves vanish when they meet the outer core, which a liquid explains. P waves slow down and bend, but they can continue.

stem: A shallow-focus earthquake has its focus
b: at the centre of the Earth
explanation: Shallow earthquakes originate in the outer tens of kilometres. For the same magnitude they often cause stronger shaking at the surface than deep ones.

stem: An earthquake under the sea is especially hazardous when it
d: displaces the seafloor and can raise a tsunami
explanation: Vertical movement of the seabed disturbs the water. Coastal areas may then face a tsunami as well as the shaking.

stem: The point where three circles of station distance meet is used to find the
explanation: Each station gives a distance from the epicentre. The common intersection of three such circles is the epicentre.

stem: Magnitude scales are logarithmic, which means that
b: each step up is a large increase in wave size, not a small equal step
c: a rise from 5 to 6 is a 1 percent change
explanation: On the original Richter scale, one unit corresponds to a tenfold increase in recorded amplitude. A magnitude 6 is not slightly larger than a 5.

stem: A magnitude 7 earthquake has a larger source than a magnitude 5 earthquake. The amplitude is greater by a factor of about
explanation: Each magnitude unit is a tenfold change in amplitude. Two units, from 5 to 7, mean 10 times 10, which is 100.

stem: Isoseismal lines on a map connect places of
explanation: An isoseismal joins locations that reported the same Mercalli intensity. The lines usually surround the epicentral area.

stem: Liquefaction during an earthquake is
a: a volcanic lava flow in every quake
c: the temporary loss of strength in a wet sandy soil, so it behaves like a fluid
d: the melting of the inner core
explanation: Shaking can raise water pressure in loose saturated sand until the grains lose contact. Buildings may then tilt or sink.

stem: The safest immediate action indoors when shaking starts is to
c: run to a doorway and then outside during the strongest shaking
explanation: Dropping under a sturdy table and holding on reduces injury from falling objects. Lifts and windows are hazards during the shaking.

stem: Pakistan's northern region is earthquake-prone mainly because it lies
a: near the collision boundary of the Indian and Eurasian plates
b: at the centre of a stable shield with no faults
explanation: The ongoing collision that raised the Himalayas and Karakoram also produces large earthquakes in the north of the country.

stem: A fault is
a: an unbroken fold with no displacement
d: a fracture along which the rocks have moved
explanation: Movement along a fracture makes it a fault. The sudden slip on a fault is what generates an earthquake.

stem: Elastic rebound explains earthquakes as
a: the daily heating of the ground
b: the pull of the tides alone
c: the sudden release of strain that rocks had stored
d: a slow leak of rain into the crust
explanation: Rocks bend as stress builds. When they break, they spring back toward a less strained shape and send out seismic waves.

stem: The instrument's heavy mass in a simple seismograph stays still while the ground moves because of
explanation: A freely suspended mass tends to remain at rest. The ground and the frame move around it, and that relative motion is recorded.

stem: Deep earthquakes are most often associated with
b: the centres of continents far from any plate edge
explanation: A sinking plate remains cold and brittle to considerable depth, so earthquakes can occur hundreds of kilometres down. Ridge quakes are shallow.

stem: The Ring of Fire is
a: a ring of deserts in Africa
c: a climate zone at the equator
d: a belt of earthquakes and volcanoes around the Pacific
explanation: Subduction around much of the Pacific produces a chain of volcanoes and frequent earthquakes. That belt is called the Ring of Fire.

stem: P waves are also called
explanation: A P wave pushes and pulls the rock in the direction of travel, which is compression and expansion. An S wave shears the rock from side to side.

stem: If a station records a very short gap between P and S,
a: the station is inside the outer core
c: the earthquake is on the opposite side of the Earth
explanation: The S wave has had little time to fall behind, so the source is close. A long gap means a distant source.

stem: Seismology is the study of
a: earthquakes and the waves they produce
explanation: Seismology uses elastic waves to study earthquakes and the interior of the Earth. It is a branch of geophysics.

stem: A tremor is
explanation: Tremor is the general word for ground shaking. It may be a small earthquake or the shaking felt from a larger one.

stem: Buildings on soft wet ground may suffer more damage because
explanation: Loose sediment can increase the amplitude and duration of shaking. Solid rock often shakes less at the same distance.

stem: The inner core is inferred to be solid partly because
a: it is cooler than the crust
b: some seismic waves that have crossed it behave as they would in a solid
c: S waves cross the outer core easily
d: no wave returns from inside the Earth
explanation: Studies of waves that pass through the centre show a solid inner core inside the liquid outer core. The outer core itself blocks S waves.

stem: An earthquake of small magnitude can still cause serious damage if it is
a: shallow and directly beneath a city
explanation: Intensity at the surface depends on depth, distance, and ground conditions, not on magnitude alone. A shallow nearby shock can be destructive.

stem: The hanging wall is
d: the block of rock above a dipping fault
explanation: On a sloping fault, the upper block is the hanging wall and the lower block is the footwall. Their relative movement defines a normal or a reverse fault.
